item.title: Roundcube CVE-2024-42009 Espionage, GitHub/NPM Supply Chain Malware, and Mount Royal Breach
item.content:encoded:
Hackers exploit Roundcube flaw to spy on academic researchers — Must Read

A likely China-aligned threat cluster is exploiting unpatched Roundcube servers at U.S. and Canadian universities to steal credentials and deploy backdoors, with a focus on physics, engineering, and national security-related research. Administrators should urgently patch CVE-2024-42009 and CVE-2025-49113 and treat exposed mail servers as critical remote-access infrastructure.

  • A China-linked threat cluster tracked by Proofpoint as UNK_MassTraction has been exploiting vulnerable Roundcube servers at U.S. and Canadian universities since May.
  • The campaign targets physics and engineering departments, administrators, professors, and organizations involved in astrophysics, particle physics, or national security-related research.
  • The attack starts with a malicious email that triggers CVE-2024-42009 in vulnerable Roundcube clients and loads IceCube, a stealer that can harvest usernames, passwords, cookies, two-factor authentication data, and browser information.
  • Proofpoint says IceCube uses helpers to exploit CVE-2025-49113 and attempts to install the SquareShell PHP webshell, while failed attempts may lead to the in-memory loading of the VShell backdoor.
  • Proofpoint assesses that UNK_MassTraction is likely a China-aligned espionage actor, but emphasizes that the attribution is not high-confidence.

Malicious Go Module Exposes GitHub Malware Lure Network Spanning 222 Repositories — Must Read

A malicious Go module posing as a DNS/subdomain scanner exposed Operation Muck and Load, a GitHub-based malware lure network of 222 repositories across 190 accounts. The campaign used fake active projects, hidden PowerShell loaders, public dead drops, password-protected archives, and RAT/infostealer payloads to target developers and users likely to run untrusted tools.

  • Researchers began with a malicious Go module, github[.]com/kaleidora/dnsub-scanning-tool, that posed as a DNS/subdomain scanner while embedding Windows malware-staging logic.
  • The Go module launched hidden PowerShell that downloaded content from muckcoding[.]com, saved it as api.db, decoded it into L.ps1 with certutil, and executed it with PowerShell execution-policy bypass.
  • The decoded PowerShell loader used public dead-drop locations, encrypted resolver material, and a hardcoded key to resolve a GitHub release URL for the password-protected Quixo.7z archive.
  • The extracted archive launched current\Microsoft.exe from C:\ProgramData\Windows.Microsoft.Photos\current\, a fake Microsoft Photos path, and the post-staging payload set was associated with RAT and infostealer-like behavior.
  • Pivoting from the module revealed 222 confirmed threat actor-workflow GitHub repositories across 190 accounts, using synthetic GitHub Actions commit activity to make lure projects look active and recently maintained.

Mount Royal University confirms breach as hackers claim attack — Should Read

Mount Royal University confirmed that attackers stole data from certain H drive folders and deleted files from both H and J drives, disrupting recovery. The CMD Organization extortion group claims responsibility and is demanding 30 BTC while threatening to leak stolen sensitive documents.

  • Mount Royal University in Calgary says hackers stole data from certain folders on its H drive and deleted original copies to disrupt recovery operations.
  • The June 17 cyberattack disrupted a broad range of university systems, including online services, internet access, and certain internal systems.
  • The affected H drive folders contained information related to current and former students, current and former university employees, and other individuals.
  • Mount Royal University says a separate J drive containing departmental data was wiped, but there is currently no evidence that its data was accessed or copied before deletion.
  • The CMD Organization threat group claimed the attack, published samples of allegedly stolen data, and demanded a 30 BTC ransom before leaking the full stolen dataset.

Fake Paysafe, Skrill SDKs on NPM and PyPi steal credentials — Should Read

Malicious npm and PyPI packages impersonating Paysafe, Skrill, and Neteller SDKs were used to steal API keys, tokens, passwords, and other secrets from developer environments. Anyone who installed the listed packages should remove them, audit dependency trees, and rotate all secrets on affected systems.

  • Malicious packages on npm and PyPI impersonated Paysafe, Skrill, and Neteller payment SDKs and delivered stealer malware to developers and users of those payment applications.
  • The threat actor published at least 17 malicious packages that exfiltrated credentials and access tokens to a command-and-control server hosted on Amazon Web Services.
  • The fake packages exposed expected APIs and returned fake success responses instead of communicating with Paysafe’s backend services.
  • Socket reported that the malware searched compromised environments for secrets including Paysafe API keys, AWS keys, GitHub tokens, npm tokens, hostnames, usernames, and API usage metadata.
  • Developers who installed any of the listed packages were advised to rotate all secrets on any machine that imported or executed them and to search dependency trees and CI logs for indicators of the campaign.

Cash App owner to pay $45 million to settle allegations of lax security — Should Read

Block, the owner of Cash App, will pay $45 million to 46 states to settle allegations that it misled users about the app’s security and failed to protect or support fraud victims. The settlement also requires Cash App to maintain live customer support and reinforces related federal restitution obligations.

  • Block, Inc., the owner of Cash App, will pay $45 million to settle allegations from 46 states that it misled users about the payment app’s security and exposed them to fraud.
  • State attorneys general said Cash App falsely promised users protections similar to a bank and failed to provide promised fraud protection and resolution required by law.
  • Investigators found that Cash App had no customer support phone number for years, leading users to find and call fake support numbers set up by scammers.
  • Investigators said Cash App did not require a Social Security number or date of birth for signup and did not limit how many accounts one person could open, allowing bad actors to operate networks of scam accounts.
  • The consent judgments require Block to maintain 24-hour live support, including at least 13.5 hours covered by a real person, and reaffirm a related federal agreement for Block to distribute $75 million to $120 million to states.

DHS Revives Critical Infrastructure Threat Sharing, Without the Legal Shield Industry Wants — Should Read

DHS has launched ANCHOR-CI to restore formal cyber and physical threat-sharing between government and critical infrastructure sectors, but it does not include the liability protections industry had under CIPAC. Health-ISAC warned that the missing legal shield may limit candid discussions about sensitive cyber incidents and vulnerabilities.

  • The Department of Homeland Security has created ANCHOR-CI as a successor to the critical infrastructure partnership system it dismantled 15 months ago.
  • ANCHOR-CI restores a formal channel for government and industry to discuss cyber and physical threats.
  • The charter establishing ANCHOR-CI omits the liability protections that participants had under the former CIPAC council.
  • Industry valued CIPAC’s liability protections because they gave executives confidence to discuss incidents in group settings without antitrust or regulatory exposure.
  • Errol Weiss of Health-ISAC said the government must address legal exposures that prevent companies from discussing sensitive cyber incidents and vulnerabilities.

Greek victims file lawsuit against Intellexa over Predator spyware — May Read

Eight Greeks allegedly targeted with Predator spyware are suing Intellexa and 13 associated individuals for about €7.6 million in damages over privacy and communications violations. The case follows Greece’s Predator scandal, prior prison sentences for Intellexa’s founder and associates, and claims by the founder that the Greek government was responsible for targeting.

  • Eight Greeks who were snooped on by Predator spyware sued Intellexa and 13 individuals tied to the company on Tuesday.
  • The victims are seeking about €7.6 million in total compensation for alleged moral damage from violations of their privacy, communications confidentiality and personal data.
  • The Predator spyware scandal became public in 2022 after traces were found on dozens of phones and led to the resignations of Greece’s intelligence service chief and the prime minister’s chief of staff.
  • Plaintiffs include a former Meta security manager, financial journalist Thanassis Koukakis, two lawyers, a former director of the Hellenic Police’s Forensic Laboratories, the former head of a Greek intelligence agency, journalist Spyridon Sideris and a former intelligence and law enforcement official.
  • Intellexa founder Tal Dilian and three associates were sentenced to more than 126 years in prison, but under Greek law they will serve only 8 years and remain free until appeals end.

Introducing Secret Exfiltration Protection for GitHub Actions — May Read

Recent supply chain campaigns show attackers are using stolen GitHub tokens to add malicious GitHub Actions workflows that dump repository secrets from CI runners. StepSecurity is introducing controls to block unreviewed workflows from accessing secrets and detect exfiltration attempts when they run.

  • The article says recent supply chain campaigns used stolen GitHub tokens to commit malicious GitHub Actions workflows that allowed CI runners to read and exfiltrate repository secrets.
  • The GhostAction campaign reached 327 users across 817 repositories and stole 3,325 secrets, including npm, PyPI, and DockerHub tokens.
  • The Megalodon campaign injected backdoored workflow files into more than 5,500 repositories in a six-hour window by targeting repositories where branch protection did not require review.
  • The Hades campaign committed a workflow named Run Copilot that used toJSON(secrets) to dump repository secrets into a file, uploaded it as an artifact named format-results, then deleted the run and branch.
  • StepSecurity’s Secret Exfiltration Policy blocks unreviewed workflows from using secrets, while Harden-Runner’s Secret Exfiltration Attempt detection flags runs with indicators such as known workflow names, toJSON(secrets), matching commit messages, and exfiltration artifacts.

From Days to Minutes: AI-Assisted Rule Writing for Threat Hunters | Corelight — Optional

Corelight argues that AI-assisted rule writing can help threat hunters turn detection ideas into usable rules in minutes instead of days, speeding up investigation and response workflows.

  • The article is from Corelight and focuses on AI-assisted rule writing for threat hunters.
  • The article presents AI assistance as a way to reduce rule-writing time from days to minutes.
  • The article’s title frames faster rule creation as useful for threat hunters.
